newsitem.title: FRANCE: Franc weaker but BoF expected to support currency.
newsitem.headline: Franc weaker but BoF expected to support currency.

text.p: The franc was weaker against the mark following the left's projected upset win in Sunday's first legislative election round but traders and economists said the Bank of France would intervene to try to stop any big fall.
"I think the Bank of France will be very quick to support the franc with intervention," said economist Sonja Gibbs of Nomura.
"The Bank of France will follow the situation very closely and will hold the cross," said a trader at a major French bank.
The franc was trading at 3.3750/55 per mark at 1920 GMT, down from 3.3714 before the voting results were announced.

Economists and traders predicted most of the impact of the left's strong showing would be felt by the three-month PIBOR contract. The left was believed to have grabbed between 40.6 and 41.6 percent of the vote, suggesting France could be heading for a period of difficult "cohabitation" between a possible left-wing government and conservative President Jacques Chirac.

"There's always more volatility on the PIBOR in this type of situation than on the franc as the franc is managed (by the central bank)," said one trader. He thought the franc could lose another 30 to 40 centimes against the mark on Monday but no more.
Economist Marie Owens-Thomsen of BIP said she did not expect the franc to go through 3.38 per mark. "Even if there is a knee- jerk reaction, I do not think it should take it through 3.38."
"I would focus on the fact that there is no more information in the first voting round than there was in the polls and that people need to wait for the second round," she said.
Others believed the franc could headed for a bigger fall.
"The franc could make a pretty rapid push toward 3.40 per mark and, depending on how quick the Bank is to come in, it could test its old two-and-a-quarter ERM band," said Gibbs.
Not only could the French currency suffer but also other European currencies "as people worry about the future of EMU (European monetary union)", she added.

Another economist, Philipe Brossard of ABN-Amro, predicted the franc could fall to 3.3850 on Monday and said the closure of financial markets in London and New York on Monday could mean a fresh wave of selling on Tuesday.
The election results "could be negative for the lira and the peseta," he said. A left victory could be "seen as negative for convergence trades".
Economist Eric Chaney of Morgan Stanley said he believed that the Bank of France would support the franc. "I do not see it falling below 3.39 although 3.39 is possible."
He said he did not expect the Bank to raise interest rates, at least during the coming week, "but things could be different after the second round".
Chaney added he believed the Socialists would continue to support monetary union. "They cannot afford to throw out EMU as their electorate is in favour of the EMU," he said.
But he said they would find it tough to strike a any kind of power-sharing deal with the Communists who oppose a single currency and want a fresh referendum on the euro.
